div.head: Af El. 28
div.ab: Gif hwa oðfæste his friend fioh, gif he hit self stæle, forgylde be twyfealdum. Gif he nyte, hwa hit stæle, geladige hine selfne, þæt he ðær nán facn ne gefremede. Gif hit ðonne cucu feoh wære, ⁊ he secgge, þæt hit here name oððe hit self ácwæle, ⁊ gewitnesse hæbbe, ne þearf he þæt geldan. Gif he ðonne gewitnesse næbbe, ⁊ he him ne getriewe, swerige he þonne.

Gif hwa oðfæste hys frynd feoh, gyf he hyt self stele, forgylde be twyfealdum; gyf he nyte, hwa hyt stæle, gá, ladige hine selfne, þæt he ðær nan facen ón ne gefremede. Gif ðonne cwicu feoh wære, ⁊ he secge, þæt hit here name oððe hyt sylf acwæle, ⁊ he gewitnesse hæbbe, ne ðearf he þæt gyldan. Gyf he ðonne gewitnesse næbbe, ⁊ he him ne getrywe, swerge he ðænne.

Gif hwa oðfæste his freond feoh, gif he hit sylf stele, forgylde be twyfealdum. Gif he nite, hwa hitt stele, geladie hine sylfne, þæt he þær nan fanc on ne fremede. Gif hit þonne cucu feoh wære, ⁊ he sæcge, þæt hit here name oððe þæt hit sylf acwæle, ⁊ he gewitnesse hæbbe, ne þearf he þæt gyldan. Gif he þonne gewitnesse næbbe, ⁊ he him getreowe ne sy, swerie he þonne.

Si quis commendauerit amico suo pecuniam uel uas in custodiam, et ab eo qui susceperat furto ablata fuerit, si inuenitur fur, duplum reddet. Si latet, dominus domus applicabitur ad deos (id est iudices) et iurabit, quod non extenderit manum in rem proximi sui ad perpetrandam fraudem tam in boue quam in asino et oue et uestimento et quicquid dampnum inferre potest, ad deos utriusque causa perueniet, et si illi iudicauerint, duplum restituet proximo suo. Si quis commendauerit proximo suo asinum, bouem, ouem et omne iumentum ad custodiam, et mortuum fuerit aut debilitatum uel captum ab hostibus, nullusque hoc uiderit, iusiurandum erit in medio, quod non extenderit manum ad rem proximi sui, suscipietque dominus iuramentum, et ille reddere non cogetur. Quodsi furto ablatum fuerit, restituet dampnum domino. Si comestum a bestia, proferat ad eum quod occisum est et non restituet. Qui a proximo suo quicquam horum mutuum postulauerit, et debilitatum aut mortuum fuerit domino non presente, reddere compelletur. Quodsi inpresentiarum fuerit dominus, non restituet, maxime si conductum uenerat pro mercede operis sui.

Gif hwa oðfæste his friend fioh, gif he hit self stæle, forgylde be twyfealdum. Gif he nyte, hwa hit stæle, geladige hine selfne, þæt he ðær nan facn ne gefremede. Gif hit ðonne cucu feoh wære, ⁊ he secgge, þæt hit here name oððe hit self ácwæle, ⁊ gewitnesse hæbbe, ne þearf he þæt geldan. Gif he ðonne gewitnesse næbbe, ⁊ he him ne getriewe, swerige he þonne.

Wenn jemand seinem Freunde Fahrhabe anvertraut: wenn dieser sie selbst gestohlen hat, vergelte er sie zwiefach. Wenn er nicht weiss, wer sie stahl, reinige er sich selbst, dass er keinen Betrug daran verübte. Wenn es aber Lebgut war, und er sagt, dass Feindesheer es fortgenommen habe, oder dass es [von] selbst gestorben sei, und er Zeugniss hat, so braucht er das nicht zu ersetzen. Wenn er jedoch kein Zeugniss hat, und jener ihm nicht traut, dann schwöre er [sich rein].

If someone entrusts movable goods to his friend: if the latter has stolen them himself, let him repay them twofold. If he does not know who stole them, let him clear himself [of the charge] that he committed any fraud in it. But if it was livestock, and he says that an enemy army took it away or that it died [of] itself, and he has witness, then he need not make it good. But if he has no witness, and the other does not trust him, then let him swear [himself clear].

If anyone entrust property to his friend, if he steal it himself, let him repay two-fold. If he knows not who stole it, let him clear himself, that he committed no fraud there. If it then were livestock, and he says that an army took it, or that it killed itself, and he has witness, he need not pay for it. If then he have no witness, and he [the owner] will not believe him, let him bring an oath.

Should someone entrust property to his friend: if he [the recipient] steals it himself, let him pay twofold restitution. If he does not know who stole it, let him submit to proof that he did no wrong. If, however, it was living property, and he should say that a troop took it or that it died on its own, and he has a witness, he need not pay for it. If, however, he does not have a witness, and he [the owner] does not believe him, let him swear.

Af setzt einen anderen Fall als Vulg.; vielleicht missverstand er invenitur fur: ‘als Dieb erfunden’ und ab als ‘durch’ statt ‘von — weg’; denn die richtige Übs. ‘ertappt wird’ hätte den Diebstahl zum handhaften, nicht mit blosser Doppelbusse sühnbaren, gemacht

Af posits a different case from the Vulg.; perhaps he misunderstood invenitur fur: as ‘found to be a thief’ and ab as ‘by’ instead of ‘away from’; for the correct transl. ‘is caught’ would have made the theft one taken in the act, not atonable by mere double compensation

Bei feindlicher Plünderung dachte Ælfred gewiss zunächst an Dänen; auch manche Urk. fasste Verheerung durch hæðen folc als mögliche Störung der Klostereinkünfte ins Auge. Vgl. Gl Zeuge 2. 11e. Hier scheint Agsä. Recht vorzuliegen; vgl. Brunner II 393; Grimm DRA 593

In speaking of hostile plundering Ælfred was certainly thinking first of the Danes; many a charter too contemplated devastation by hæðen folc as a possible disruption of a monastery’s revenues. Cf. Gl Zeuge 2. 11e. This appears to be Anglo-Saxon law; cf. Brunner II 393; Grimm DRA 593

On Alfred as a law-giver, see pp. 326 f. The code was probably issued late in his reign. The introduction shows that Alfred had acquired some proficiency in translating from Latin or had scholars to help him, and his account of the Apostles’ letter and of synods held in later days may be influenced by the letter he received from Fulk about 885 (No. 223). The code, with Ine’s laws following it, survives complete in the mid-tenth-century MS. C.C.C.C. 173 and in the twelfth-century Textus Roffensis, and, in Latin, in Quadripartitus. The twelfth-century MS. C.C.C.C. 383 has lost the early part, and only fragments remain of the early-eleventh-century MS. B.L.Cott. Otho B. xi, but of this there is a transcript made by Nowell (B.L.Addit. MS. 43703). Only the capitula and the beginning of the introduction survive in B.L.Cott. Nero A. 1, and only a fragment of Ine’s laws in B.L.Burney MS. 277. Alfred’s and Ine’s laws were used in later laws. I give only a selection from Alfred’s introduction, and I omit some chapters on tariffs. The code is edited in full by Liebermann, I, 15–89, and by Thorpe, 1, 44–101, with translation; Attenborough, pp. 62–93, has a translation but omits almost all of Alfred’s introduction.
